column4: Arctic regional reanalysis on single levels from 1991 to present
column5: The C3S Arctic Regional Reanalysis (CARRA) dataset offers 3-1 hours analyses and 1 hours short-term forecasts of various atmospheric and surface meteorological variables. These include surface and near-surface temperature, surface and top of atmosphere fluxes, precipitation, cloud cover, humidity, wind, pressure, snow, and sea-related variables, all at a high spatial resolution of 2.5 km. The dataset is divided into two domains: West domain: Covers Greenland, the Labrador Sea, Davis Strait, Baffin Bay, Denmark Strait, Iceland, Jan Mayen, the Greenland Sea, and parts of Svalbard. East domain: Covers Svalbard, Franz Josef Land, Novaya Zemlya, Barents Sea, and the northern parts of the Norwegian Sea and Scandinavia. CARRA has been developed using the HARMONIE-AROME non-hydrostatic regional numerical weather prediction model. High-resolution reanalysis for the Arctic is crucial due to the pronounced effects of climate change in this region, necessitating detailed descriptions beyond those provided by global reanalyses like ERA5. Inputs to the CARRA reanalysis include observational data, the ERA5 global reanalysis for lateral boundary conditions, and physiographic datasets describing the model's surface characteristics. The combination of observational values and their quality information is used to constrain the reanalysis in areas with available observations and to inform the data assimilation system in less observed regions.

column4: ERA5-Land 1 hours data from 1950 to present
column5: ERA5-Land is a reanalysis dataset offering a detailed and consistent view of the evolution of land variables over several decades, with enhanced resolution compared to ERA5. This dataset has been created by replaying the land component of the ECMWF ERA5 climate reanalysis. Reanalysis merges model data with global observations using physical laws to produce a comprehensive dataset that accurately describes past climate conditions. ERA5-Land uses ERA5 atmospheric variables, such as air temperature and humidity, as input to control the simulated land fields. This atmospheric forcing prevents model-based estimates from deviating significantly from reality. Although observations are not directly used in ERA5-Land production, they indirectly influence the dataset through the atmospheric forcing. Additionally, corrections are made to input air temperature, humidity, and pressure to account for altitude differences between the forcing grid and the higher resolution ERA5-Land grid, a process known as 'lapse rate correction'. Like any simulation, ERA5-Land provides estimates with some degree of uncertainty. Numerical models can only approximate the real physical processes governing different Earth System components. Generally, the uncertainty of model estimates increases as we go back in time due to fewer available observations for creating a high-quality atmospheric forcing. ERA5-Land parameter fields can be used in conjunction with the uncertainty of equivalent ERA5 fields.

column4: ERA5-Land 1 month averaged data from 1950 to present
column5: ERA5-Land is a reanalysis dataset that offers a detailed and consistent view of land variables over several decades, with enhanced resolution compared to ERA5. It has been created by replaying the land component of the ECMWF ERA5 climate reanalysis, which integrates model data with global observations using the laws of physics. This process results in a globally complete and consistent dataset that accurately describes past climate conditions. ERA5-Land provides a comprehensive view of the water and energy cycles at the surface level from 1950 onwards, with a temporal resolution of 1 hour. The native spatial resolution is 9 km on a reduced Gaussian grid (TCo1279), but the data available in the Climate Data Store (CDS) has been regridded to a regular lat-lon grid of 0.1x0.1 degrees. The dataset presented here is a post-processed subset of the full ERA5-Land dataset. To facilitate applications that do not require sub-1 month fields, 1 month-mean averages have been pre-calculated for easy and fast access.

column5: This dataset comprises a set of land surface parameters derived from the Noah 3.6.1 model within the Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) Land Data Assimilation System (FLDAS). The data are provided at a resolution of 0.10 degrees and cover the period from January 1982 to the present day. Temporally, the data are presented on a 1 month basis, with global spatial coverage extending from 60 degrees South to 90 degrees North and from 180 degrees West to 180 degrees East. It's worth noting that the FLDAS regional 1 month datasets are now obsolete and have been replaced by the global 1 month dataset. The simulation process utilized a blend of Modern-Era Retrospective Analysis for Research and Applications version 2 (MERRA-2) data and Climate Hazards Group InfraRed Precipitation with Station (CHIRPS) 6-1 hours rainfall data, downscaled using the NASA Land Data Toolkit. Initialization of the simulation occurred on January 1, 1982, employing soil moisture and other state fields sourced from a FLDAS/Noah model climatology corresponding to that specific day of the year. A significant update in November 2020 involved the post-processing of all FLDAS data using the MOD44W MODIS land mask. Previously, certain grid boxes over inland water were erroneously treated as land, leading to non-missing values. The post-processing rectified this by masking out all model output data over inland water bodies. It's important to note that this post-processing didn't impact the meteorological forcing variables. Further details on this update can be found in the FLDAS README document, and the MOD44W MODIS land mask is accessible on the FLDAS Project site. Users who obtained FLDAS data before November 2020 are advised to re-download the data to access the post-processed version.

column5: The 1 month anomaly dataset features land surface parameters simulated by the Noah 3.6.1 model within the Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) Land Data Assimilation System (FLDAS). Each 1 month file represents the deviation of that month from the 35-year 1 month climatology spanning from 1982 to 2016. This comparison is based on the FLDAS Noah Land Surface Model L4 Global 1 month 0.1 x 0.1 degree (MERRA-2 and CHIRPS) V001 (FLDAS_NOAH01_C_GL_M_001) 1 month data. The spatial resolution is set at 0.10 degrees, and coverage extends globally (from 60 degrees South to 90 degrees North and from 180 degrees West to 180 degrees East). It's noteworthy that the FLDAS regional 1 month anomaly datasets are now obsolete, having been replaced by the global 1 month anomaly dataset. For further insights into the 1 month FLDAS dataset, users are encouraged to refer to the dataset landing page for FLDAS_NOAH01_C_GL_M_001 and the FLDAS README document. In November 2020, all FLDAS data underwent post-processing with the MOD44W MODIS land mask. Previously, certain grid boxes over inland water were erroneously treated as land, resulting in non-missing values. The post-processing rectified this by masking out all model output data over inland water bodies. Importantly, this post-processing didn't affect the meteorological forcing variables. Additional information on this update can be found in the FLDAS README document, and the MOD44W MODIS land mask is accessible on the FLDAS Project site. column5: This dataset comprises a series of land surface parameters simulated using the Noah 3.6.1 model within the Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) Land Data Assimilation System (FLDAS), adapted from the Land Information System (LIS7). It includes 28 parameters presented at a spatial resolution of 0.10 degrees, covering the period from January 2019 to the present. Temporally, the data are provided on a 1 month basis, with global coverage extending from 60 degrees South to 90 degrees North and from 180 degrees West to 180 degrees East. The simulation process was driven by a combination of Global Data Assimilation System (GDAS) data and Climate Hazards Group InfraRed Precipitation with Station Preliminary (CHIRPS-PRELIM) 6-1 hours rainfall data, which was downscaled using the NASA Land Data Toolkit. The simulation was restarted from CHIRPS-FINAL data of the previous month. Initialization of the simulation occurred on January 1, 2019, utilizing soil moisture and other state fields from a FLDAS/Noah model climatology corresponding to that specific day of the year.

column5: The NASA Global Land Data Assimilation System Version 2 (GLDAS-2) comprises three distinct components: GLDAS-2.0, GLDAS-2.1, and GLDAS-2.2, each serving specific purposes within the system. GLDAS-2.0, extending from 1948 to 2014, relies solely on Princeton meteorological forcing input data, ensuring temporal consistency throughout the dataset. GLDAS-2.1, operational from 2000 to the present, incorporates a blend of model and observational data, offering a comprehensive approach to land surface data assimilation. GLDAS-2.2 introduces a new paradigm by incorporating data assimilation (DA) techniques. Unlike its predecessors, GLDAS-2.2 harnesses the power of assimilating data from various sources, leading to enhanced accuracy in its outputs. The specifics of forcing data, DA observation sources, variables, and schemes employed vary across different GLDAS-2.2 products. GLDAS-2.2 is new to the GES DISC archive and currently includes a main product from CLSM-F2.5 with Data Assimilation for the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE-DA) from February 2003 to present. The GLDAS-2.2 data are available in two production streams: one with GRACE data assimilation outputs (the main production stream), and one without GRACE-DA (the early production stream). Since the GRACE data have a 2-6 month latency, the GLDAS-2.2 data are first created without GRACE-DA, and are designated as the Early Product (EP), with about 1 month latency. Once the GRACE data become available, the GLDAS-2.2 data are processed with GRACE-DA in the main production stream and are removed from the Early Product archive. This data product is an Early Product for GLDAS-2.2 Catchment Land Surface Model 1 day 0.25 x 0.25 degree with GRACE-DA. The GLDAS-2.2 GARCE-DA product was simulated with Catchment-F2.5 in Land Information System (LIS) Version 7. The data product contains 24 land surface fields from February 1, 2003 to present. The simulation started on February 1, 2003 using the conditions from the GLDAS-2.0 1 day Catchment model simulation, forced with the meteorological analysis fields from the operational European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) Integrated Forecasting System. The total terrestrial water anomaly observation from GRACE satellite was assimilated (Li et al, 2019). Due to the data agreement with ECMWF, this GLDAS-2.2 1 day product does not include the meteorological forcing fields. The GLDAS-2.2 data are archived and distributed in NetCDF format.

The GLDAS-2.1 data are archived and distributed in NetCDF format. The GLDAS-2.1 simulation started on January 1, 2000 using the conditions from the GLDAS-2.0 simulation. This simulation was forced with National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)/Global Data Assimilation System (GDAS) atmospheric analysis fields, the disaggregated Global Precipitation Climatology Project (GPCP) V1.3 1 day Analysis precipitation fields, and the Air Force Weather Agency's AGRicultural METeorological modeling system (AGRMET) radiation fields. In October 2020, all 3-1 hours and 1 month GLDAS-2 data were post-processed with the MOD44W MODIS land mask. Previously, some grid boxes over inland water were considered as over land and, thus, had non-missing values. The post-processing corrected this issue and masked out all model output data over inland water; the post-processing did not affect the meteorological forcing variables. column5: The Modern-Era Retrospective Analysis for Research and Applications, Version 2 (MERRA-2), starting from 1980, replaces the original MERRA with improved assimilation systems, accommodating modern observational data such as hyperspectral radiance and GPS-Radio Occultation datasets. It also incorporates NASA's ozone profile observations since 2004. Maintaining a spatial resolution of about 50 km, MERRA-2 is the first global reanalysis to assimilate aerosol observations and represents interactions with other climate processes. Additionally, it includes representations of ice sheets over regions like Greenland and Antarctica. M2T1NXLND (or tavg1_2d_lnd_Nx) represents an 1 hours time-averaged 2-dimensional dataset within MERRA-2. This compilation encompasses various land surface diagnostics including baseflow flux, runoff, surface soil wetness, root zone soil wetness, water content at the surface and root zone layers, as well as soil temperature across six layers. Each data entry is timestamped with the central time of an hour, commencing from 00:30 UTC. This dataset spans from 1980 to the present, with an approximate latency of three weeks after each month's conclusion.

column5: This dataset comprises a collection of land surface parameters simulated using the Mosaic land-surface model (LSM) for Phase 2 of the North American Land Data Assimilation System (NLDAS-2). The data are spatially resolved with a grid spacing of 1/8th degree and cover the time span from January 1979 to the present. Temporal resolution is provided at 1 hours intervals, and the file format utilized is WMO GRIB-1. The Mosaic model, developed by Koster and Suarez in 1994 and 1996, adopts a tile approach to account for subgrid vegetation variability. Each vegetation tile encapsulates its own energy and water balance, as well as soil moisture and temperature characteristics. Within NLDAS, Mosaic is configured to accommodate a maximum of 10 tiles per grid cell, with a 5% threshold to exclude vegetation classes covering less than 5% of the cell. Additionally, in the NLDAS context, all tiles within a grid cell exhibit a predominant soil type and are characterized by three soil layers with fixed thickness values of 10, 30, and 160 cm, leading to a constant rooting depth of 40 cm and a consistent total column depth of 200 cm. The Mosaic LSM is driven by 1 hours NLDAS-2 forcing files denoted as \File A

column5: This dataset consists of a series of land surface parameters simulated using the Noah land-surface model (LSM) for Phase 2 of the North American Land Data Assimilation System (NLDAS-2). The data are provided with a 1/8th degree grid spacing and cover the period from January 1979 to the present. Temporally, the data are presented at an 1 hours resolution. The file format utilized is WMO GRIB-1. For detailed information on the NLDAS-2 configuration of the Noah LSM, readers are directed to Xia et al. (2012). The Noah model was originally developed as the land component of the NOAA NCEP mesoscale Eta model. For its application in NLDAS-2, recent modifications have been made to Noah's cold-season and warm-season parameterizations. Noah also serves as the land component in various atmospheric models including the evolving Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) regional model, the NOAA NCEP coupled Climate Forecast System (CFS), and the Global Forecast System (GFS). The model incorporates simulations of the soil freeze-thaw process and its effects on soil heating/cooling and transpiration. It comprises four soil layers with spatially invariant thicknesses of 10, 30, 60, and 100 cm, with the first three layers forming the root zone in non-forested regions, while the fourth layer is included in forested regions. The Noah LSM is forced by the 1 hours NLDAS-2 forcing \File A\" files and contains fifty-two fields. A user-defined parameter table is utilized to indicate the contents and parameter number. The GRIBTAB provides a comprehensive list of parameters for this dataset

column5: The Smerge-Noah-CCI root zone soil moisture 0-40 cm L4 1 day 0.125 x 0.125 degree V2.0 dataset is a comprehensive multi-decadal product offering information on root-zone soil moisture. Developed by integrating data from the North American Land Data Assimilation System (NLDAS) land surface model and surface satellite retrievals from the European Space Agency Climate Change Initiative, this dataset provides a 1 day time-step resolution at a 0.125-degree spatial resolution. Covering the entire continental United States, it spans nearly four decades from January 1979 to May 2019. Key features of this dataset include root-zone soil moisture values for the 0-40 cm layer, Climate Change Initiative (CCI) derived soil moisture anomalies for the same layer, and a soil moisture data estimation flag for quality assessment.

column5: This dataset offers global estimates of surface soil moisture derived from a comprehensive collection of satellite sensors. Developed using the methodology from the ESA Climate Change Initiative for Soil Moisture, it represents the cutting edge of satellite-based soil moisture climate data record production. The dataset adheres to the ?Systematic observation requirements for satellite-based products for climate? established by the Global Climate Observing System (GCOS). The data are provided on a regular latitude/longitude grid, with potential gaps in spatial and temporal coverage. In the context of satellite data, references to Climate Data Records (CDR) and interim-CDR (ICDR) are common. For this dataset, both CDR and ICDR components were produced using the same software and algorithms. The CDR is designed to be long enough, consistent, and continuous to monitor climate variability and change. The ICDR offers timely access to current data, maintaining consistency with the CDR baseline, though it may not have undergone extensive validation. column5: The production of the FLDAS Central Asia dataset, known as product FLDAS_NOAH001_G_CA_D v001, will cease on September 30th, 2023. We advise users to transition to the FLDAS2 Central Asia dataset, denoted as product FLDAS_NOAHMP001_G_CA_D. This dataset encompasses a range of land surface parameters simulated via the Noah 3.6.1 model within the Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) Land Data Assimilation System (FLDAS), adapted from the Land Information System (LIS7). Featuring 23 parameters, the dataset offers a spatial resolution of 0.01 degrees covering the Central Asia region (30-100°E, 21-56°N). It spans 1 day observations from October 2000 (Water Year 2001) to the present day. The simulation process primarily relies on Global Data Assimilation System (GDAS) data. To ensure stable snow and soil conditions, a nine-year spin-up of the Asia-LIS system was conducted. Model states were compared against MODIS Maximum Snow Extent data for validation during the spin-up period, and adjustments were made to establish a climatological model state for October 1st. Subsequently, the Asia-LIS model was executed from October 1st, 2000 to September 30th, 2011, generating 1 day outputs. Model states were reset to the climatological state on October 1st of each year to ensure consistency in surface states at the onset of each hydrologic year.

column4: Essential climate variables for assessment of climate variability from 1979 to present
column5: The Essential Climate Variables for Assessment of Climate Variability from 1979 to Present dataset includes a curated selection of climatologies, 1 month anomalies, and 1 month mean fields of Essential Climate Variables (ECVs) that are ideal for monitoring and assessing climate variability and change. This dataset prioritizes variables based on their accuracy and temporal consistency over 1 month to decadal time scales. The ECV data products are derived from climate reanalyses such as ERA-Interim, ERA5, and ERA5-Land. Depending on the source, these data may have been adjusted to correct biases and other known deficiencies, with details on data sources and adjustment methods provided in the Product User Guide. The guide also specifies the baseline periods used to calculate 1 month climatologies and the corresponding anomalies. The dataset provides various statistical measures, including 1 month average fields, climatologies, anomalies, and 12-month running mean anomalies. Climatologies and anomalies are calculated relative to two reference periods: 1981-2010 (for ERA5, ERA5-Land, and ERA-Interim) and 1991-2020 (for ERA5 and ERA5-Land).

column5: The Modern-Era Retrospective Analysis for Research and Applications, Version 2 (MERRA-2), starting from 1980, replaces the original MERRA with improved assimilation systems, accommodating modern observational data such as hyperspectral radiance and GPS-Radio Occultation datasets. It also incorporates NASA's ozone profile observations since 2004. Maintaining a spatial resolution of about 50 km, MERRA-2 is the first global reanalysis to assimilate aerosol observations and represents interactions with other climate processes. Additionally, it includes representations of ice sheets over regions like Greenland and Antarctica. M2TMNXLND (or tavgM_2d_lnd_Nx) represents a 1 month mean dataset of time-averaged 2-dimensional land surface diagnostics within the MERRA-2. This dataset encompasses various parameters including baseflow flux, runoff, surface soil wetness, root zone soil wetness, water content at the surface and root zone layers, soil temperature across six layers, as well as variance of select parameters. Covering the period from 1980 to the present, this dataset typically becomes available with a latency of approximately three weeks after the conclusion of each month.

column5: The NASA Global Land Data Assimilation System Version 2 (GLDAS-2) comprises three distinct components: GLDAS-2.0, GLDAS-2.1, and GLDAS-2.2, each serving specific purposes within the system. GLDAS-2.0, extending from 1948 to 2014, relies solely on Princeton meteorological forcing input data, ensuring temporal consistency throughout the dataset. GLDAS-2.1, operational from 2000 to the present, incorporates a blend of model and observational data, offering a comprehensive approach to land surface data assimilation. GLDAS-2.2 introduces a new paradigm by incorporating data assimilation (DA) techniques. Unlike its predecessors, GLDAS-2.2 harnesses the power of assimilating data from various sources, leading to enhanced accuracy in its outputs. The specifics of forcing data, DA observation sources, variables, and schemes employed vary across different GLDAS-2.2 products. This data product, reprocessed in January 2020, is for GLDAS-2.1 Noah 3-1 hours 0.25 degree data from the main production stream and it is a replacement to its previous version. The 3-1 hours data product was simulated with the Noah Model 3.6 in Land Information System (LIS) Version 7. The data product contains 36 land surface fields from January 2000 to present. The GLDAS-2.1 data are archived and distributed in NetCDF format. The GLDAS-2.1 products supersede their corresponding GLDAS-1 products. The GLDAS-2.1 simulation started on January 1, 2000 using the conditions from the GLDAS-2.0 simulation. This simulation was forced with National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)/Global Data Assimilation System (GDAS) atmospheric analysis fields (Derber et al., 1991), the disaggregated Global Precipitation Climatology Project (GPCP) V1.3 1 day Analysis precipitation fields (Adler et al., 2003; Huffman et al., 2001), and the Air Force Weather Agency's AGRicultural METeorological modeling system (AGRMET) radiation fields. The simulation used with GDAS and GPCP only from 2000 to February 2001, followed by addition of AGRMET for March 1, 2001 onwards. In October 2020, all 3-1 hours and 1 month GLDAS-2 data were post-processed with the MOD44W MODIS land mask. Previously, some grid boxes over inland water were considered as over land and, thus, had non-missing values. The post-processing corrected this issue and masked out all model output data over inland water; the post-processing did not affect the meteorological forcing variables. More information can be found in the GLDAS-2 README. The MOD44W MODIS land mask is available on the GLDAS Project site.

column5: This dataset includes (1) 1 month measurements of soil CO2 efflux, volumetric water content, and temperature, and (2) seasonal measurements of soil properties (such as porosity, bulk density, nitrogen and carbon content) and vegetation characteristics (like leaf area index (LAI), litter, and fine root biomass) in a water-limited ecosystem in Baja California, Mexico. Data collection took place from August 2011 to August 2012. The research was conducted in El Mogor, located in the Valle de Guadalupe, Baja California, Mexico. The sampling area covered 100 x 50 meters, with 50 sampling points spaced 5 to 10 meters apart. Additionally, the enhanced vegetation index (EVI) was derived for a 2 x 2 km area centered on the study site using the MODIS Land Product Subsets (MOD13Q1) to complement the 1 month vegetation measurements.
